QF.id: XIII Introduction to the Underlying Markets_72

question.text: If a currency is said to be at a 'forward premium,' what does this indicate?

answer.text: The forward quote for that currency is higher than its spot rate for the given pair, reflecting the interest-rate differential between the two currencies under no-arbitrage pricing
The currency can only be bought at a premium above the market price
The central bank has imposed a surcharge on forward transactions
The currency is trading above its purchasing power parity value

explanation.text: The Logic: A currency is at a forward premium when its forward rate is higher than its spot rate for the relevant pair. For example, if USDINR forward is above USDINR spot, USD is at a forward premium to INR (and INR is at a forward discount to USD). The source frames this premium/discount as the outcome of the interest-rate differential under a no-arbitrage relationship. The Trap: Forward premium is not about trading restrictions, central-bank surcharges or purchasing power parity. It is also not a forecast of future spot appreciation — it is a pricing relationship driven by interest-rate differentials. Note: The same forward-premium concept underpins corporate hedging economics: hedging costs and benefits for importers and exporters are largely a function of this premium/discount, not of any directional view on future spot.
